report:
## Conclusion

The evidence on ginkgo biloba extract for tinnitus is mixed and, on balance, not convincing. The Cochrane systematic review (four trials, 1,543 participants) found no reliable evidence that ginkgo reduces tinnitus severity compared with placebo (cochrane.org). Individual randomized trials have produced conflicting results: some smaller/older studies and a meta-analysis of select trials suggested modest benefit, while the largest, best-designed placebo-controlled trial to date (Rejali et al., 2004) found no benefit over placebo (pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3157487/). Reflecting this inconsistent and generally weak evidence base, the American Academy of Otolaryngology–Head and Neck Surgery Foundation's Clinical Practice Guideline explicitly recommends that clinicians should NOT recommend ginkgo biloba (or other dietary supplements) as a treatment for persistent, bothersome tinnitus (ata.org/about-tinnitus/is-there-a-magic-pill/).

More recent exploratory, open-label studies using the standardized EGb 761® extract (120 mg twice daily) have reported symptomatic improvement in chronic tinnitus patients, but these were uncontrolled (no placebo group) and thus prone to placebo effect and regression to the mean, limiting their ability to prove a true drug effect (mdpi.com/2077-0383/15/1/87).

**Bottom line:** Despite decades of study, rigorous randomized controlled trials and systematic reviews have not established that ginkgo biloba reliably relieves tinnitus symptoms beyond placebo. It appears generally safe, so some people may try it, but major clinical guidelines advise against recommending it as a tinnitus treatment. Anyone considering it should discuss with a physician, especially given possible interactions with blood-thinning medications.
